summary: Told of Galileans killed by Pilate at their sacrifices, Jesus calls His hearers to repent, and tells of a barren fig tree given one more year.
key_insight: Jesus’ hearers brought Him one disaster, and He added another they had not mentioned: a tower that fell in Jerusalem. One came from a ruler’s cruelty, the other from an accident, and Jesus gave both the same answer: “I tell you, no; but unless you repent you will all likewise perish.”
story: At that time some people told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices.

Jesus answered them, “Do you suppose that these Galileans were worse sinners than all other Galileans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, no; but unless you repent you will all likewise perish.”

Then He raised another case Himself: “Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them, do you think that they were worse sinners than all other men who dwelt in Jerusalem?” Again He said, “I tell you, no; but unless you repent you will all likewise perish.”

He told them a parable. A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came looking for fruit on it and found none. So he said to the keeper of his vineyard, “Look, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and find none. Cut it down; why does it use up the ground?”
But the keeper answered, “Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it. And if it bears fruit, well. But if not, after that you can cut it down.”

scene.label: Pilate and the Galileans
scene.text: Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36. No other record mentions this killing, but the Jewish historian Josephus tells of other times Pilate sent soldiers against Jewish crowds. Sacrifices were offered only at the temple, so these Galileans died in Jerusalem, probably while on pilgrimage for a feast.

scene.label: The tower in Siloam
scene.text: Siloam was the area at the south end of Jerusalem around the pool of that name (John 9:7). The tower may have been part of the city wall there. Nothing else is known of its collapse; it was recent news Jesus could mention without explaining.

scene.label: A fig tree in a vineyard
scene.text: Farmers often planted fig trees among their vines, and sitting “under his vine and under his fig tree” was Israel’s picture of peace (Micah 4:4). A fig tree drew heavily on the soil. Digging around it and spreading manure was extra care, a last effort to bring fruit.

scene.label: Israel and the fig tree
scene.text: The prophets spoke of Israel as God’s vineyard, planted with care and expected to bear fruit (Isaiah 5:1–7), and God said He had found Israel’s fathers like “the firstfruits on the fig tree” (Hosea 9:10). Jesus’ hearers would hear their nation’s story in the parable as well as their own.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records these two disasters and the parable. They follow straight on from Jesus’ call to discern “this time” and to settle accounts before reaching the judge (12:54–59): the hour is urgent, and the delay is mercy. Matthew and Mark tell of a fig tree cursed in Holy Week (Mark 11:12–14); Luke has no such scene, and his parable leaves the barren tree with one more year.

seeing.reveals: Jesus refuses to read tragedy as a scorecard of who is worse. He speaks with urgency and with patience together: the axe is ready, yet the owner grants another year of digging and care.
seeing.living: When disaster falls on others, the question is not what they did but what you must do. Every tragedy in the news is a call to the living to turn to God while there is time. Do not mistake the extra year for a permanent reprieve.
seeing.ponder: What fruit has God been looking for in your life, year after year, that He has not yet found?

preaching.big_idea: Tragedy is not a verdict on others but a warning to us: repent while mercy waits.
outline: A tragedy and a wrong conclusion (1–3)
A second tragedy, the same warning (4–5)
A barren tree and a patient keeper (6–8)
preaching.watch_for: Jesus repeats the same sentence word for word (vv. 3, 5). The parable then shows what the owner is looking for, which is fruit, and why judgment has not yet fallen: the keeper asked for “this year also” (v. 8).
